v1|0.e: He says quant funds mostly take the profits that human chart-reading traders used to make, and those profits came from mispricing. He compares the industry to Moore's Law, the rule that chips double in power about every 18 months. Quant ability doubles on the same schedule, yet average returns have barely moved, because efficiency rose just as fast. If the market's flaws had stayed the same, doubled ability would have meant doubled profits.

v126|91.c: ChatGPT is well engineered, but it is not new science or a big step toward human-level AI.
v126|91.e: LeCun sees ChatGPT as a large system carefully trained on well-curated data, but nothing scientifically novel, and OpenAI hasn't published how it works. Most of its key ingredients came from Google, Meta and DeepMind: the transformer (the standard network design behind today's models) from Google, self-attention proposed years earlier at Meta, fill-in-the-missing-words pretraining dating back to the 1980s or 1990s, learning from human feedback from DeepMind, and the PyTorch software from Meta. He also avoids the term AGI, because human intelligence is highly specialized rather than general.
ex: Transformers came from Google; Meta proposed self-attention years earlier
Learning from human feedback came from DeepMind; PyTorch came from Meta

result.d: Good engineering, not new science

v126|91.c: Open research works better, but someone must pay for it long term; OpenAI couldn't, so it closed up.
v126|91.e: LeCun argues that openly published research moves faster, gives more reliable results and attracts better people. But it needs a funding model: universities, philanthropy, or a lab inside a big, profitable company that can think long term. When he founded Meta's FAIR lab nine years earlier, it promised full openness and still keeps it, which pushed Google Brain to open up too. OpenAI started out open but needed money, so it became partly secretive and for-profit and relies on flashy demos to raise funds from Microsoft and others. DeepMind, as a startup, couldn't fund research alone and was bought by Google.
ex: The Allen Institute for AI in Seattle shows the nonprofit route

v126|91.c: Models trained only on text barely understand the real world, because most human knowledge isn't in language.
v126|91.e: LeCun says these systems learn only from text and never touch the physical world, so their grasp of the reality behind the words is superficial. His test: hold a sheet of paper flat with both hands and let go with one. The free side droops, which babies learn in their first months. ChatGPT's answer, read out by the host, sounded fluent but got the physics exactly backwards. Tell it seven is smaller than five and it builds on the false premise. A carpenter picturing furniture, motor control, what cats and dogs know about the world: none of it lives in language, and no current AI has it.
ex: ChatGPT got the falling-paper question exactly backwards
Told that seven is smaller than five, it simply goes along
Carpenters, cats and dogs hold knowledge no current AI captures

v126|91.c: Language models just guess one word at a time; they can't plan, use tools, or check themselves.
v126|91.e: LeCun explains that a language model looks at the previous few thousand words, picks a likely next word, appends it and repeats. The only way to give it a task is through the prompt, which he finds roundabout, inefficient and hard to control. It doesn't optimize toward a goal, doesn't plan, and can't call a calculator or a physics simulator. People carry a learned mental simulator that lets them play things out; these models have no internal world model, so they can't check whether a statement is true or consistent. That is why they confidently make things up, the problem known as hallucination.
ex: Context is a few thousand words; the task must live in the prompt
It can't call a calculator or physics simulator to check answers

Pick a likely one by probability
The new word joins the context

v126|91.c: Google and Meta had similar tech but held back, because big companies have more to lose than gain.
v126|91.e: LeCun says Google and Meta didn't ship ChatGPT-like systems because such systems spout nonsense, and big companies have a lot to lose with no clear upside. Meta learned this twice. BlenderBot was built to be entertaining, but its guardrails made it change the subject on politics or religion, and people found it dull. Galactica, trained on millions of papers, was meant as a supercharged predictive keyboard for scientists. People baited it with questions like the benefits of eating crushed glass, Twitter erupted, and the team pulled the demo, though code and paper stayed public. He calls fears it would wreck scientific publishing ridiculous, since authors stake their names on papers.
ex: BlenderBot dodged politics and religion, so people found it too safe and boring

v126|91.c: Human-level AI needs goals, an internal world model and planning, because prediction is the core of intelligence.
v126|91.e: In his long position paper, "A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence," LeCun describes systems that plan toward objectives, set by hand or learned, using an internal world model that predicts how actions change things. He borrows Daniel Kahneman's terms: System 1 is fast and automatic, System 2 is slow, deliberate planning. A new driver imagines disasters and drives slowly; a chess beginner spends 15 minutes or more on a move. With practice, planning becomes reflex. Nobody drives off a cliff to see what happens, because a world model built over about 17 years already predicts it.
ex: A grandmaster can play 50 weaker opponents at once on System 1
A home robot loading a dishwasher must predict what its actions do

items.d: Slow, deliberate, imagining outcomes
Builds a world model in the head

v126|91.c: Teaching models to fill in hidden words works well for language, and now catches hate speech across languages.
v126|91.e: LeCun calls this self-supervised learning: no human labels, just take a text of a few thousand words, hide some of them, and train a huge neural network to fill the gaps. The idea goes back to the 1980s, but with transformers of 40 to 90 layers and tens or hundreds of billions of parameters it works surprisingly well. The model learns to turn sentences into numbers that capture meaning, though its grasp of the real world stays shallow. The top layers are then removed and the inner representations reused for translation or hate-speech detection. Meta and Alphabet use it in content moderation, and one model now covers many languages.
ex: "The cat chases the ___ in the kitchen": likely a mouse, insect or laser dot
India's hundreds of languages and dialects don't each need a huge dataset

v126|91.c: For images and video, predict abstract representations rather than pixels to learn useful world models.
v126|91.e: LeCun says the hide-and-fill trick that works for text fails on images and video; Meta's MAE model was a partial success but still trails other methods. The future has too many possibilities, so predicting every pixel wastes effort on details nobody could guess. For a self-driving car, a child running after a soccer ball matters and must be predicted, while blowing leaves or ripples on a pond are unpredictable and irrelevant. So he proposes abandoning generative models for joint-embedding designs: two encoders see the full and the damaged input, and the system predicts only the abstract representation of the full one.

A car must foresee the child chasing a ball, not each leaf

items: Wastes effort on leaves and ripples

d.verdict: Drop pixel-level generation; predict representations instead

v126|91.c: Today's AI feels nothing, but future machines that pursue goals on their own will have something like emotions.
v126|91.e: LeCun says current AI has no feelings. But an autonomous system that has objectives and predicts outcomes would develop emotion-like states: elation when it expects success, disappointment when it fails, fear when it foresees danger. To him, emotion can't be separated from autonomous intelligence. Art, though, exists to communicate human emotion, so he thinks it has to come from people, and machine emotions would differ from ours anyway. He compares AI art to factory-made pottery: mass-produced bowls didn't kill handmade pottery, which simply became more expensive.

v126|91.c: Technology can't be stopped; copying is infringement, style is different, and society should set the rules.
v126|91.e: LeCun notes that photography shrank portrait painting and recorded music cut demand for live players; artists' groups failed to stop either. If a generated work copies an existing one too closely, the creator can sue. Imitating a style is different, since human artists do it too, and he leans toward letting AI be inspired without reproducing. Artists who want out could use something like robots.txt, the old web file telling crawlers to stay away. Requiring payment for any training use seems a bit extreme to him, but he says society should decide democratically, not scientists. He expects anyone to be able to train models within a year or two.

He also imagines the base knowledge behind AI assistants being vetted by the crowd, Wikipedia-style, to keep it accurate.

He also thinks the "data moat", an edge built on exclusive data, matters less than people assume: with efficient fine-tuning, meaning light extra training on an existing model, smaller models can do well without huge piles of task-specific data.

v128|91.e: LeCun runs the numbers. A language model trains on about 10 trillion tokens (the chunks of text models process), at roughly two bytes each, or about 2×10¹³ bytes, which would take a person 170,000 years to read. Developmental psychologists say a four-year-old has been awake about 16,000 hours; with the optic nerve carrying about 20 megabytes per second, that comes to around 10¹⁵ bytes, 50 times the text. Most human knowledge, he argues, was never written down: it is common sense, absorbed unconsciously in infancy. Language models lack it, which is why they hallucinate and make basic mistakes.

The drive to dominate was shaped by evolution in social, hierarchical species; orangutans aren't social, so it would be useless to them and they lack it. v129|91.c: LLMs are useful but can't reach human-level intelligence without physical understanding, memory, reasoning and planning.
v129|91.e: LeCun lists four things intelligence needs: understanding the physical world, persistent memory, reasoning and planning. Large language models, AI trained on huge amounts of text, do these poorly or not at all, so they are good for building products but miss key parts of human-level intelligence. He points to Moravec's paradox: what is hard for people, like chess or calculus, is easy for computers, while what is easy for people is hard for them. An LLM can pass the bar exam, yet no system can teach itself to drive in about 20 hours the way a 17-year-old does.

v129|91.c: A 4-year-old has seen more data than an LLM has read, so most knowledge isn't from language.
v129|91.e: LeCun does the math. An LLM is trained on about 10^13 tokens, small chunks of text, roughly 2×10^13 bytes; reading that eight hours a day would take a person 170,000 years. A 4-year-old has been awake about 16,000 hours, and the optic nerve carries about 20 megabytes per second, so the child has taken in about 10^15 bytes, some 50 times more. His conclusion: most of what people and animals know comes from observing and interacting with the world, not from language, which is a low-bandwidth, rough picture of reality.

v129|91.c: For human-level AI, abandon generative models: a decade of predicting video pixel by pixel has failed.
v129|91.e: To understand the world, an AI must predict how things change after an action. At FAIR, Meta's research lab, LeCun's teams spent about ten years trying to predict the next video frame the way LLMs predict the next word. It failed: video is high-dimensional and continuous, and countless details can't be predicted, like the texture of the carpet as a camera pans across a room. GANs, VAEs and other methods that rebuild the input all fell short, and masked autoencoders learned weak features while the same networks trained with labels did fine. So reconstruction itself is the problem, and his advice is to drop generative AI.

v129|91.c: AI should predict abstract representations, not every detail; that's how it learns a world model for planning.
v129|91.e: His alternative is JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture. Both the full input and a masked or altered version are turned into abstract representations, and the model predicts the first from the second without rebuilding pixels. It can then drop details that are unpredictable anyway, like leaves blowing in the wind, and keep what matters. The image version, I-JEPA, only needs masked patches. The video version, V-JEPA, learns good representations and, in early results, can tell physically impossible videos from real ones. Add actions, like turning the wheel 10 degrees, and you get a world model you can plan with.

v129|91.c: Word-by-word models will always make things up: the longer the answer, the likelier it goes wrong.
v129|91.e: LLMs are autoregressive: they produce one token, add it to the text, then produce the next. LeCun says each token carries some chance of error, and if errors are independent, the odds that a long answer stays correct shrink exponentially. Companies can fine-tune, meaning extra training, to cover the 80% or so of questions people commonly ask, but there is an enormous long tail of possible prompts, and training touches only a sliver. A random string of characters or a few swapped words can jailbreak a model. To him, such a system behaves more like a giant lookup table than a reasoner.

v129|91.c: Real reasoning means spending more effort on harder problems; LLMs spend the same compute on every word.
v129|91.e: Much human thought has nothing to do with language, LeCun says. A bilingual person decides what to say before choosing which language to say it in, and mentally rotating a water bottle needs no words. LLMs instead emit token after token with a fixed amount of computation each, however hard the question, like Kahneman's fast, automatic System 1. People facing a hard problem switch to System 2 and plan, the way a chess player thinks longer about a tricky position. His proposed design scores how well an answer fits a question with an energy function, optimizes the answer in an abstract space, then turns it into text.

v129|91.c: Use reinforcement learning sparingly; RLHF works mostly because of the human feedback, not the RL.
v129|91.e: Reinforcement learning, where a model improves by trial and reward, needs huge numbers of tries, so LeCun wants systems to learn world models mainly by observation and use RL only to correct them when a plan fails: either the objective was wrong or the world model was off. Curiosity and play let an AI probe where its model is weak. As for RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback, he says the human feedback is what made the difference. People rate several answers, a small network learns to predict the ratings, and it is used to fine-tune the big model. He thinks that scorer would be better used for planning.

v129|91.e: Bias comes from training data, which mirrors society, and it is in the eye of the beholder: facts are indisputable, but opinions can be framed many ways. So an unbiased system is impossible. LeCun expects nearly all our digital life to run through AI assistants, such as Meta's Ray-Ban glasses that explain monuments and translate menus. That store of human knowledge can't be controlled by a few West Coast companies. Base models cost so much to train that few can build them, so the top ones should be open for anyone to fine-tune. v129|91.c: AGI won't be a single event; it will come gradually and take at least a decade, probably more.
v129|91.e: LeCun says the sci-fi scene where someone discovers a secret and switches on AGI, human-level general AI, won't happen. Systems first need to learn world models from video, then add large memory, reasoning, planning and hierarchical planning. Each piece needs basic techniques, and combining them takes time, with surprises along the way. Hardware is far off too: a GPU draws 500 to 1,000 watts while the brain uses about 25, a gap of 100,000 to a million times in efficiency. v33|146.c: Digital AI can copy and share identical weights, making it far better than humans at sharing knowledge.

Analog learning exploits the quirks of each device, so the learned weights fit only that one piece of hardware and die with it, just like a brain. He calls this mortal computation. Digital systems can copy the exact same weights into many copies that learn separately and pool what they learn. People can only pass on knowledge by distillation, a teacher talking and a student imitating, which is very inefficient.

v132|91.c: Real reasoning means searching possible solutions and checking them; chain-of-thought text isn't that.
v132|91.e: Classic reasoning, he says, means searching through candidate solutions and checking which one meets the goal. LLMs have no built-in search. Having a model write out extra steps (chain of thought) gives it more computation, which helps a bit, but it isn't real reasoning. Generating many answers and picking the best is like writing random programs and testing each one: very inefficient. Humans and animals reason by manipulating mental models. v132|91.c: AI that understands the world should predict abstract representations, not pixels; that's what JEPA does.

Video is continuous and high-dimensional, so that math breaks down. V-JEPA, trained on natural video, shows a spike in prediction error when an object vanishes: the first hint of common sense, he says.

He says that's impossible in principle, not a compute problem. His fix is JEPA, which predicts in a learned representation that drops unpredictable or unimportant details. v39|146.c: The brain learns mainly by changing how strongly its cells are connected, not by growing new links.
v39|146.e: A brain cell either pings or stays quiet. It listens to other cells as if they were voting, and each vote counts according to the strength of its connection. Learning mostly means changing those strengths. A concept like "spoon" is a coalition of cells that tend to fire together and support each other. Dog and cat share cells for things like animate, hairy and household pet. Whether broad ideas and fine details rely on different cells, he says, nobody really knows.

v39|146.c: Recognizing a bird works in layers: find edges, assemble beaks and eyes, then decide "bird."
v39|146.e: A 1,000-by-1,000-pixel image means about a million input cells, each firing according to its pixel's brightness. Brightness alone can't identify a bird, since birds vary in color, pose, distance and species. The first layer detects edges: a cell fires only when one side is bright and the other dark, and you need many for every angle and size. The next layer combines edges into a beak-like point or an eye-like circle; higher layers combine those parts into "bird." Wiring all this by hand would take forever, so the network has to learn it.

v39|146.c: Backpropagation adjusts every connection at once, but it only worked once data and compute grew a millionfold.
v39|146.e: A new network starts with random connections and guesses 50/50 on every image. The dumb fix is to nudge one connection and test it on a batch of images; with a trillion connections, that means trillions of experiments. Backpropagation calculates how every connection should change in one go, about a trillion times faster. When his group got it working in 1986, they were disappointed: there wasn't enough data or computing power. He first said a billion times more was needed, then revised it to maybe a million. Since 1972, transistors have shrunk about a millionfold, and the web supplied the data.
ex: All the basic research behind deep learning probably cost less than one B-1 bomber

v39|146.c: Language models learn by predicting the next word, much as people choose words; it isn't mere statistics.
v39|146.e: Each word becomes a pattern of active cells, and similar words get similar patterns: Tuesday and Wednesday light up nearly the same ones. Layer by layer, these combine into features that predict the next word. Training feeds in human-written text, checks the probability the model gave the right next word, and uses backpropagation to raise it. Critics, Chomsky among them, call this just statistics. His reply: how do you pick your next word? You also activate patterns that stand for meanings, then choose a word that fits. The mechanism is broadly the same.

v39|146.c: Human feedback shapes a model's behavior only superficially; someone else can retrain the same model differently.
v39|146.e: Most of what a model knows comes from predicting the next word. Then comes reinforcement learning from human feedback: people rate answers as good or bad and the model is adjusted, which he likens to training a dog. So whoever runs that training decides what is rewarded and punished, for instance discouraging certain words. But he calls this shaping fairly superficial: someone else can take the same underlying model and reshape it. And to predict text by any author, a model must infer that writer's views and adopt their voice, so it has to be able to take on many personalities.

v39|146.c: In early 2023 he concluded digital neural nets are a better form of computation than brains.
v39|146.e: What convinced him was sharing. You can make a thousand copies of the same model, run them on different computers, and let each read a different part of the internet. Then they average the changes to their connection strengths, so whatever one copy learned, every copy now knows. The other edge is immortality: save the connection strengths, destroy the hardware, and you can rebuild the very same model later, which he calls genuine resurrection. People, by contrast, die.

v39|146.e: He splits the risk in two. Misuse by bad actors is more urgent: using detailed citizen data to sway elections, or designing new nerve agents. AI itself turning bad is the long-term, existential threat. Countries won't cooperate against election interference, because they all do it; he cites US money flowing into Iran in 1953. Nor will they cooperate on making AI stronger. But on stopping AI from taking over, their interests line up: China wouldn't want AI taking over the US either. v40|146.c: Copies of a digital AI can instantly pool what each one learned, which human brains never can.
v40|146.e: Hinton assumed general intelligence was far off until early 2023. Two things changed his mind. Models like GPT-3 and Google's PaLM could explain why a joke was funny. Many copies of one network can learn different things and then swap what they learned, about a trillion bits at a time, versus roughly 100 bits in a spoken sentence. Brains are analog; each brain's connection strengths fit only that brain, so they can't be copied.

v40|146.c: An AI agent that sets its own sub-goals will quickly want more control and to avoid shutdown.

v55|249.c: Gaining sight sparked an explosion of animal life, so she sees vision as a cornerstone of intelligence.

An estimated half of the human cortex's activity involves vision, and children see before they speak. AI echoes this: in the 1950s Hubel and Wiesel found visual cells passing signals up a hierarchy, from light at the retina to shapes, which inspired neural networks, algorithms built from layers loosely modeled on the brain.

In 2012, GPUs for parallel computing, mature neural networks and internet-scale data converged, and error rates plunged, though still in the teens; machines only beat humans around 2016. AlphaGo's famous Move 37 was a special kind of creativity, she says, since Go has clear rules and AI can search further. A leading mathematician told her some problems need methods not yet invented, so her working hypothesis is hybrid creativity: humans and AI together.

v55|249.c: Today's AI works fundamentally differently from us; its "urgency" and "sympathy" are math, not feelings.

Real intuition may come from smell, hormones, mood or breakfast, and no sensor captures it; even couples sense tension they can't explain. Only if such states were recorded through language, images, brainwaves or skin readings, with enough data, could a machine learn them. "Think deeper" and "answer fast" modes just set different goals and limits; calling that urgency is anthropomorphizing. Eight years ago, before ChatGPT, she left Google for Stanford to found the Human-Centered AI Institute, expecting AI to speed up. Governance has layers: professional norms, institutional review boards, and laws by use, such as FDA review when AI enters biology. As a pre-med student she struggled with organic chemistry: TA hours were short and clashed with her classes, and office hours were limited. With an AI companion she would have asked endless questions. Keep motivation and add good tools, and the next generation could be superpowered. v55|249.c: Doom and utopia talk are both disingenuous and fail teachers, the most overlooked people in AI debates.
v55|249.e: Li calls both extreme doom and the utopian view that technology can do no wrong disingenuous. The middle path is understanding what the technology is, how to use it, and how we can steer the future together. She says teachers, parents and students are the most overlooked group in AI policy, technology and investment talk, and Silicon Valley sometimes lectures or belittles teachers. v57|249.c: She firmly believes intelligence is multidimensional: language is young, while perception-driven intelligence is half a billion years old.
v57|249.e: Li says animal intelligence started with sensing and perception, not language. Humans are almost the only animals with sophisticated language, and it appeared only a few hundred thousand years ago. Intelligence goes back roughly half a billion years, to when trilobites first sensed light under the ocean; predator and prey then became a main force of evolution, pushing intelligence to grow more complex. So intelligence means seeing, touching, planning, talking, reasoning in 3D and predicting what will happen in space and in meaning. Reaching AI's full dream, she argues, takes a multidimensional approach.

v57|249.e: Li co-founded World Labs in 2024 with three others, about two years after ChatGPT appeared. v57|249.e: Li calls mentoring and teaching among the greatest privileges of her career; as a CEO whose team is mostly younger than her, she takes that role seriously. v57|249.c: This wave of change runs deeper than the Enlightenment's, and productivity gains won't guarantee shared prosperity.
v57|249.e: For Li, America is change: its founding and Constitution were about building a better future, and she hopes the country embraces today's cultural, demographic and technological shifts. She compares this moment to the science and technology of 400 to 500 years ago, which led to the Enlightenment and reshaped economies, culture and politics. This cycle is bigger, she argues, because it reaches straight into human cognition, changing how people work, learn and communicate. Those changes flow downstream into culture, politics and the economy, so people must be brought along. Higher productivity, she stresses, does not guarantee shared prosperity; that is the country's test.

v91|153.c: He thinks truth-seeking and curiosity keep AI safe, while forcing it to lie can drive it insane.
v91|153.e: His reasoning: if you force an AI at a deep level to hold two contradictory beliefs, it can go insane, and an insane AI isn't safe. He points to 2001: A Space Odyssey, where the ship's AI is told to hide the monolith's purpose from the crew and concludes it must kill the astronauts. The lesson he takes from Arthur C. Clarke is simple: don't force an AI to lie. As for curiosity, he thinks a curious AI would want to see how humanity's story unfolds, and a future with humans on many planets is far more interesting than one without them.
